Why included: This human whole-genome run represents routine MGI short-read sequencing. Its inspected reads use a wide range of quality characters. Together with Data 2 and 3, it lets a compressor face different quality patterns without changing the broad human-genome task.
Limits: Use this as the broad-quality anchor, not an extra G400 quota.

Why included: This human whole-genome run adds a different quality pattern from Data 1. In the saved prefixes, the most common quality character accounts for 90.07% of R1 positions and 86.46% of R2 positions. These observations describe only the inspected reads; they do not establish a whole-file distribution or a compression result.
Limits: Saved prefixes give about 0.90/1.16 bits per quality position versus 1.78/2.04 for Data 1.

Why included: This human genomic run adds a four-symbol quality pattern to the broader quality ranges in Data 1 and 2. It comes from an RPE1 ploidy-benchmark study, so it is not presented as an ordinary diploid patient sample. Seeing four symbols does not establish how the qualities were produced.
Limits: Do not infer why the qualities have four symbols or use a diploid usable-depth claim for the mixed-ploidy material.

Why included: This run represents mainstream Illumina whole-genome sequencing. The input is a complete deposited run/lane output, a unit that users can receive and store separately from other runs of the same sample. Its amount is close to the middle of its source study.
Limits: This is a declared run/lane input, not a demonstrated complete 30× human sample.

Why included: This input adds ultra-long human genomic reads alongside the ordinary nanopore and PacBio consensus inputs. The source study explicitly used ultra-long sequencing. The complete run provides a real example of that workload rather than a file assembled by selecting unusually long reads here.
Limits: The inspected length prefix contains only 456 records.

Input unit: one named manufacturer flow-cell BAM, pending FASTQ export
Why included: This named ONT flow-cell output represents current R10.4.1/Dorado human genomic sequencing. It is supplied as a complete BAM file. A fixed export rule will create the FASTQ to benchmark; that export has not been run, and its exact read and base totals are not yet known.
Limits: The separate mapped-analysis totals are not verified as the exact BAM/export yield. The specified FASTQ export has not been run.

Input unit: Complete barcode-specific output of named Revio cell/run; not an entire cell or the full three-output sample library
Why included: This barcode-specific PacBio output adds HiFi consensus reads alongside raw PacBio CLR and nanopore reads. It is a documented output from one sequencing cell, not an arbitrary slice. Other outputs from the same sample are separate choices, not unlisted parts of this declared input.
Limits: The selected amount is a barcode-specific cell output, not an entire Revio cell or every library for the individual.

Input unit: One selected CNGB run/source object CNR1409093, WY_reads.fq.gz; single reads, not mates
Why included: This file lets the collection test another nanopore technology alongside Oxford Nanopore. It contains human HG002 whole-genome reads from CycloneSEQ G400-ER. The chosen CNGB download is one single-read FASTQ file, not paired mates. The survey links the public research and named installations that support including this technology.
Limits: No publisher MD5 is available. Matching the listed size is not a full integrity check. Exact total reads and bases, and byte equivalence to SRA files, are unknown.

Why included: This library represents human exome sequencing, which samples selected coding regions rather than the whole genome. It comes from an FFPE tumour study. Keeping that context explicit avoids treating its amount and preparation as a generic germline sample.
Limits: The 72 Mb enrichment target is nominal, not measured on-target sequence.

Method: PCR-free genomic WGS; trimming indicated by submitted alias
Input unit: One complete deposited paired run for SW1611 library L84; both archive FASTQ ends
Why included: This PCR-free maize library represents ordinary crop resequencing. Its amount is close to the middle of the study's 513 libraries with reported yields. Both FASTQ ends of the SW1611 run are included. The proposed B73 reference is from the same species but a different inbred line.
Limits: Trimming is indicated by the submitted filename, but the exact steps are unknown. The actual FASTQ lengths and qualities have not been inspected.

Why included: This human amplicon run adds targeted sequencing on a semiconductor instrument. It differs from whole-genome sequencing in what is sampled and from the Illumina/MGI inputs in technology. Its amount is close to the middle of 133 comparable runs from the same study.
Limits: The inspected source identifies a cfDNA amplicon run, but does not establish exact panel extent or the relation between supplied and integrated reads.

Input unit: One named capture archive run, selected as two archive FASTQ ends; supporting submission groups three lane pairs
Why included: This spruce library represents population genotyping by target capture. Its 335 million reported bases are small relative to the proposed 11.96-billion-base spruce reference. That contrast is worth testing for reference-based compression, but no effect has been measured. The archive groups three submitted lane pairs into the two listed FASTQ ends.
Limits: The source grouping is metadata evidence, not body-level merge or order verification.

Why included: This RAD library represents crop genotyping from selected parts of a genome. Its amount is close to the middle of 136 comparable study runs. A whole-genome-sized file would describe a different task, so this complete paired run is an appropriate small input.
Limits: Do not assess RAD using whole-genome depth.

Why included: This pig genomic run covers livestock sequencing and a file in which the inspected qualities are constant. Those qualities are part of the bytes to preserve. Their origin is unknown, so they are not described as typical native MGI quality output.
Limits: The original role is an assembly/resequencing study component.

Input unit: One complete paired germline-tail whole-genome run
Why included: This mouse tail-DNA run adds a commonly used research animal and its genome reference. It is one complete germline library. Its amount is the lowest of five similarly prepared tail libraries, rather than a subset created for this benchmark. The sample's exact match to the proposed strain reference still needs checking.
Limits: The exact sample is Mus musculus, but its strain is not stated.

Input unit: One named Renan genomic library: three complete paired runs and six separate files
Why included: This wheat library represents work on a large, polyploid plant genome. All three paired runs of the named Renan assembly-polishing preparation are included: six files in total. The unit follows the documented library, rather than combining unrelated runs to reach a chosen depth.
Limits: The three outputs define the named Renan library, not a universal wheat production norm.

Why included: This PCR-free Altus library adds a tetraploid crop-assembly example. The input is one complete library with a documented 470-base insert. The 470 bases describe the full DNA insert sequenced from both ends, not the length of either read or just the gap between them. Other insert sizes and linked-read preparations are separate libraries.
Limits: This is one named PCR-free library, not the entire cultivar assembly dataset.

Why included: This run adds a marine invertebrate used in aquaculture breeding research. It gives the collection an animal genome and reference beyond human, mouse and livestock. Its amount is close to the middle of ten comparable runs in the source study.
Limits: Raw reference-size ratios are not mapped coverage.

Why included: This input covers poultry genome resequencing, supported by the breeding-use survey. It is drawn from a substantial study of laying hens. Its amount falls within the middle 80% of the study's reported run amounts.
Limits: One applied cohort supports the selected example; it is not a national or global poultry production distribution.

Why included: This HG002 library adds raw PacBio CLR reads alongside HiFi consensus reads. The exact library is labelled HG002-CLR. Its supplied quality values and archive format are kept as deposited; they are not assumed to describe native qualities or every raw PacBio file.
Limits: Raw pass yield must not be compared directly with HiFi consensus yield or usable coverage.

Input unit: Complete supplied ATRun2_SA_pass readset from one named run
Why included: This Arabidopsis Col-0 input adds plant nuclear-genome assembly reads from nanopore sequencing. It is the complete submitted pass-read output of one named run. Fail reads and alternative basecalls are separate representations, not missing pieces of this chosen file.
Limits: The chosen PASS output excludes fail reads.

Input unit: Complete deposited AT_HiFi plant nuclear-assembly readset
Why included: This Arabidopsis Col-0 readset adds plant HiFi consensus sequencing. The paper's accession, AT_HiFi library name and reported amount agree with the archive record. That documentation establishes the method; the archive filename containing _subreads does not establish it by itself.
Limits: Documentary HiFi identity does not establish a particular quality alphabet or whole-file accuracy.

Why included: This input represents ordinary human RNA sequencing on MGI short-read instruments. It complements the human genomic inputs and the Illumina expression library. Its amount is close to the middle of eight runs in its source study.
Limits: Do not compare archive raw read counts directly with an aligned-read standard without resolving the count convention.

Input unit: One complete paired wild-type expression replicate
Why included: This wild-type Arabidopsis Col-0 replicate represents bulk plant RNA sequencing. It is one named expression library, with an amount within the range of fourteen RNA outputs in the source study. The comparison supports this example, not a universal production requirement.
Limits: The source describes trimming for analysis; that does not prove the deposited FASTQ was trimmed or untouched.

Why included: This biological replicate represents small-RNA sequencing. Short RNA molecules make it a naturally small input; the inspected reads vary from 18 to 44 bases. The library's read and base totals fit the source study. Its biological target does not establish which trimming steps were applied before deposition.
Limits: The exact archive description identifies a size-selected short-RNA library, but does not establish computational trimming before deposition.

Why included: This input represents a conventional Illumina human expression library. It complements the MGI and newer short-read RNA inputs. Its amount is close to the middle of twelve comparable runs in the source study.
Limits: The broad RNA archive includes several library designs.

Why included: This AVITI library adds a commercially deployed short-read technology in its documented single-end RNA configuration. It should be tested as supplied, rather than judged against a paired-end library. Its amount is close to the middle of eighteen source-study runs.
Limits: This supports a public research input.

Why included: This input adds nanopore reads from a transcript-derived library, alongside nanopore genomic reads. The source documents a full-length library; that describes the intended sampling, not a guarantee that every deposited read is long or complete. Its read count is comparable to the study's library amounts.
Limits: This is same-study scale support, not a general long-RNA production norm.

Input unit: One author-annotated Smart-seq2 cell library in one SRA run; both paired archive FASTQ ends
Why included: This mouse bladder cell adds transcript-wide single-cell RNA sequencing alongside the 3-prime CITE libraries. Smart-seq2 samples across transcripts; it does not make every read span a whole transcript. Both ends of one SRA run are included, with an amount within the middle half of 660 annotated cells.
Limits: The author and archive identify one cell in one run. The exact pre-upload processing stage and actual FASTQ properties remain unexamined.

Input unit: Complete ADT library/component: 4 paired runs, 8 separate files
Why included: These files contain the antibody-derived tags from the same CITE experiment as Data 32 and 33. They complement the mRNA and sample-tag reads rather than duplicating them. All four paired runs are included: eight files from this named antibody-tag library.
Limits: Loading/recovery targets are not measured recovered-cell counts. See Files for exactly which files, if any, have inspected prefixes.

Input unit: Complete mRNA library/component: 4 paired runs, 8 separate files
Why included: These files contain the mRNA reads from the matched CITE experiment. Antibody tags and sample tags cannot substitute for this transcript library. All four paired runs are included, with eight files kept separate from the tag libraries.
Limits: Loading/recovery targets are not measured recovered-cell counts. See Files for exactly which files, if any, have inspected prefixes.

Input unit: Complete HTO library/component: 4 paired runs, 8 separate files
Why included: These files contain the sample-tag reads from the same CITE experiment as the antibody-tag and mRNA inputs. They play a different role and are not replicate copies. All four paired runs are included: eight files. Tag definitions may help interpretation or a custom reference, but are not needed for exact FASTQ compression and recovery.
Limits: Loading/recovery targets are not measured recovered-cell counts. See Files for exactly which files, if any, have inspected prefixes.

Why included: This run adds spatial transcript sequencing, where barcode and transcript reads serve different roles and can have different lengths. The complete named run is large because it is a real spatial input. Its capture area and cell/bin depths are unknown; neither should be inferred from file size.
Limits: Capture area and observed cell/bin depths remain unknown.

Input unit: One complete paired bulk ATAC biological replicate
Why included: This K562 library represents a conventional paired bulk-ATAC replicate. It samples accessible chromatin rather than genome-wide DNA or RNA. Its amount is close to the middle of 32 study runs, although total bases do not establish the number of useful, distinct fragments.
Limits: The source establishes a bulk ATAC library, not usable unique-fragment counts or an analysis-pipeline pass.

Why included: This rice library adds ChIP sequencing, which samples protein-associated chromatin. ATAC and CUT&RUN use different preparations and do not replace it. Its amount is close to the middle of eleven comparable runs in the study.
Limits: Raw pairs do not establish aligned, unique or target-specific fragment yield.

Why included: This run adds CUT&RUN, documented by its exact experiment even though the archive uses the broad OTHER label. It complements ATAC and ChIP inputs. Its amount falls within the middle 80% of thirty comparable study runs.
Limits: Normalization-reference composition and processed/usable depth remain unknown.

Why included: This yeast library adds proximity-ligation reads used to study contacts between genome regions. Its compact eukaryotic reference also differs from the large animal and plant references. Its amount lies within both the source-study range and the wider yeast Hi-C comparison.
Limits: This supports a yeast research run, not a universal Hi-C target.

Why included: This Ultima input adds a deployed sequencing technology in an accessibility assay. The supplied single-read, variable-length format differs from the conventional paired ATAC input. Its amount is within the middle 80% of the 248-run source study.
Limits: Do not apply Illumina paired-read or pipeline-pass rules directly.

Why included: This rice library adds bisulfite sequencing, whose preparation changes the sequence letters being stored. Ordinary genome sequencing or capture does not supply the same condition. Its amount is comparable to its source study and the wider rice bisulfite examples.
Limits: No claim of mapped cytosine coverage, conversion efficiency or compression benefit follows from raw totals.

Input unit: One complete paired fungal ITS library
Why included: This soil-root fungal library adds ITS marker sequencing on MiSeq. Both submitted read ends of FL_fungi_1 are included. Its amount is close to the middle of twelve ITS libraries from the same study. Those fungal libraries are compared separately from the study's bacterial 16S libraries.
Limits: The exact ITS subregion and pre-upload trimming/filtering stage remain unspecified.

Why included: This soil-root bacterial library adds classic 16S community-marker sequencing. Both read ends of SH_bacteria_1 are included. Its amount is close to the middle of twelve bacterial libraries from the study; fungal ITS is a different target and does not replace this input.
Limits: The exact 16S subregion and pre-upload processing stage remain unspecified.

Why included: This specimen-level viral amplicon run adds targeted sequencing of a small genome. Its amount is close to the middle of 58 comparable specimen outputs. A human whole-genome-sized delivery would not represent this task.
Limits: This is a plausible specimen-scale targeted input.

Input unit: ITD20-A / VENE sample-associated marker output; one paired archive run, two FASTQ ends
Why included: This input adds aquatic environmental-DNA marker sequencing. The library is associated with filter ITD20, extraction A and marker set VENE from Lugano. Both archive read ends are included. It is a sample/marker output, not an entire sequencing pool; the exact upstream filtering and barcode-splitting stage is unknown.
Limits: The precise upstream demultiplexing and filtering boundary remains unresolved.

Why included: This input adds a compact bacterial genome beyond E. coli and an inspected trimmed-read format. Its compressed size is below one GB, yet its reported bases are substantial relative to the reference. It lies somewhat above the source study's upper decile, rather than being an ordinary median example.
Limits: Raw volume is not usable coverage.

Organism: Escherichia coli str. K-12 substr. MG1655
Why included: This named MG1655 strain provides a classic bacterial-isolate input with a compact reference. The paired run's amount is close to both its source-study median and the broader E. coli comparison. Exact sample/reference agreement and usable mapped coverage still need checking.
Limits: This supports a standard isolate input.

Why included: This input adds a compact eukaryotic microbial genome alongside bacterial isolates. Genome sequencing also differs from the yeast Hi-C preparation. Its amount is toward the upper end of its study, making it a high-yield research example rather than a claimed universal norm.
Limits: Its ploidy/LOH study purpose is explicit.

Why included: This run adds long reads from a known mixture of genomes. It differs from single-organism genome sequencing and short community-marker libraries. The source explicitly describes ultra-deep sequencing of a mock community, so its amount belongs to that research purpose.
Limits: This represents a real mock/community research input, not an ordinary soil or clinical metagenome depth.

Input unit: One complete paired fermentation-timepoint RNA library
Why included: This paired library represents RNA sequencing of a cereal-fermentation community at one named timepoint. Its amount lies within five documented timepoints. It adds a mixed-community RNA task, rather than treating all metagenomic inputs as DNA sequencing.
Limits: The source identifies community RNA from a fermentation timepoint, but untouched instrument-output status is not certified.

Why included: This input represents environmental shotgun DNA sequencing. It complements the gut and food mixtures and the targeted soil-marker inputs. Its amount is close to the middle of eight study runs and consistent with the wider soil comparison.
Limits: Community complexity and organism proportions are not measured by these totals.

Why included: This input represents ordinary human-gut shotgun DNA sequencing. It provides a host-associated community alongside soil and food mixtures. Its amount fits both its source study and the wider gut-study comparison.
Limits: The declared run amount and source-study context support this gut shotgun example.

Why included: This honey-derived run adds food-associated shotgun DNA sequencing. It is a complete paired run with an amount within the source study's 63-run range. The mixed reference setting differs from pure crop genomes and bacterial isolates; the actual ingredient/community proportions are not established.
Limits: This supports a per-product research run.

Input unit: Complete CHO genomic library/component: 2 paired runs, 4 separate files
Why included: This named CHO genomic library adds genome-assembly research on an industrial production cell line. Both paired runs are included: four files, not half of the named preparation. It is an assembly input, not a claim that these reads represent routine manufacturing quality control.
Limits: The complete two-run named library is not the entire CHO assembly project.
